selection_rule: Every statement by an in-scope officeholder quoted in a story published on Nov. 16 or 17, 2026 in the NPR Politics and PBS NewsHour Politics feeds, and in the Senate floor speeches printed in the Nov. 16, 2026 Congressional Record, as read on Nov. 17 at about 7:20 ET, less the stories the Nov. 15 and Nov. 16 pages already used. PBS NewsHour carries Associated Press reporting. One NPR story listed in the feed had no readable text and was skipped. Quotes under five words were left out, as were commentators' accounts of what an official said. Statements are worded as the outlet reported them unless a transcript is linked; entries beginning "Reported as" are the reporter's wording.
lede: This page lists 111 statements by 13 officeholders, drawn from NPR and PBS NewsHour stories and from Senate floor speeches printed in the Congressional Record for Nov. 16. They concern judicial and executive nominations, an energy permitting bill and data centers, the war in Ukraine, the farm bill, Nvidia and chip exports to China, the Nov. 13 nationwide air traffic ground stop, the federal deficit and the Senate Democratic leadership race.

80 statements could be checked. None has been checked yet; all 80 are marked not yet checked and will be updated as their checks return. Unsettled means evidence was found but does not decide the claim; unsupported means no evidence was found, not that the statement is false.

The remaining 31 statements are opinions, predictions, promises and personal attacks. They are listed because they were said, not because they can be checked. 2 pairs of statements by different officeholders are linked as counter-statements.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Speaking on November 16 about the nationwide FAA ground stop of Friday, November 13, which officials attributed to a router installed by a contractor.
statements.quote: Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.
statements.test: True if the FAA's or DOT's account attributes the Nov. 13 ground stop to failure of aging equipment. False if the official account attributes it to something other than old equipment, such as new equipment or contractor work. Cannot be determined if no official account of the cause is found.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Speaking on November 16 about the nationwide FAA ground stop of Friday, November 13, which officials attributed to a router installed by a contractor.
statements.quote: They did a great job, Secretary Duffy. They acted incredibly.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Speaking on November 16 about the nationwide FAA ground stop of Friday, November 13, which officials attributed to a router installed by a contractor.
statements.quote: Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt, no crashes, no nothing.
statements.test: True if no injuries, accidents or crashes connected to the Nov. 13 ground stop are recorded by the FAA or NTSB. False if any injury, accident or crash connected to it is recorded. Cannot be determined if no official account addresses safety outcomes.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Speaking on November 16 about the nationwide FAA ground stop of Friday, November 13, which officials attributed to a router installed by a contractor.
statements.quote: they should have done this with a system that's probably, on average, 50 years old.
statements.test: True if an official or GAO account puts the average age of the relevant air traffic control systems at around 50 years. False if official figures put it far below that. Cannot be determined if no figure for average system age is found; 'probably' allows rough agreement.

statements.speaker: Sean Duffy
statements.context: Explaining on November 16 why the FAA's work on a copper-to-fiber upgrade at a facility in southern Arkansas preceded the November 13 nationwide ground stop.
statements.quote: This was a remote facility, in Arkansas, and we didn't anticipate that this could take down the system, which is why it was done during the day.
statements.test: True if the FAA's account says the work preceding the ground stop was at a facility in Arkansas and was done during the day. False if the official account places it elsewhere or at night. Cannot be determined if no official account gives the facility or time.

statements.speaker: Sean Duffy
statements.context: Speaking on November 16 about FAA procedures after the November 13 nationwide ground stop caused by a router installation.
statements.quote: Well, we're going to review all the our whole procedures on when we do this work, how we do this work, so the system doesn't go down.

statements.speaker: Sean Duffy
statements.context: Responding to Democratic questions about the $12.5 billion Congress appropriated in 2025 for air traffic control upgrades.
statements.quote: I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom.
statements.test: True if the law appropriating the $12.5 billion, or DOT's spending plan for it, commits all of it to purposes other than new telecommunications architecture. False if the law or plan provides funds usable for a new telecommunications architecture. Cannot be determined if neither the law nor the plan can be read.

statements.speaker: Sean Duffy
statements.context: Responding to Democratic questions about the $12.5 billion Congress appropriated in 2025 for air traffic control upgrades.
statements.quote: I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s.
statements.test: True if official accounts say the FAA's core air traffic management software dates to the 1990s. False if they date it otherwise. Cannot be determined if no official account of the software's age is found.

statements.speaker: Sean Duffy
statements.context: On November 16 Duffy said he would send lawmakers a breakdown of what his $50 billion request for air traffic control upgrades would pay for.
statements.quote: Reported as: Secretary Duffy said he planned to send a breakdown to lawmakers as soon as today, detailing what his $50 billion ask would pay for.

statements.speaker: Jim Himes
statements.context: Speaking on CBS to Transportation Secretary Duffy about the $12.5 billion Congress appropriated in 2025 for air traffic control upgrades.
statements.quote: that's sitting in your bank account right now?
statements.test: Assesses only the premise, not the suggestion that funds be spent first. True if DOT, FAA or GAO figures show that most of the $12.5 billion was not yet spent (outlaid) by mid-November 2026. False if most had been spent. Cannot be determined if no spending figure is found.
statements.premise: Much of the $12.5 billion Congress appropriated in 2025 for air traffic control upgrades remained unspent in mid-November 2026.

statements.speaker: Jim Himes
statements.context: Speaking on CBS about Transportation Secretary Duffy's request for $50 billion more for air traffic control upgrades.
statements.quote: How about if you spend that before we -- we put more money in that bank account?

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: The 2026 deficit came in at a stunning $2 trillion. That represents 6.2 percent of the Nation's gross domestic product.
statements.test: True if CBO or Treasury reports the fiscal 2026 federal deficit at about $2 trillion and about 6.2 percent of GDP. False if the reported figures differ materially. Cannot be determined if no fiscal 2026 figure is published.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: Over the six decades spanning since the end of World War II, the deficit never once exceeded 6 percent of GDP.
statements.test: True if the deficit stayed at or below 6 percent of GDP in every fiscal year of the six decades after World War II (fiscal 1946 through about 2008). False if any of those years exceeded 6 percent. Cannot be determined if the historical series cannot be read.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: Yet over the past 7 years, annual deficits have exceeded 6 percent of GDP five times.
statements.test: True if the deficit exceeded 6 percent of GDP in five of fiscal years 2020 through 2026. False if it did so in a different number of those years. Cannot be determined if the yearly figures cannot be read.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: They have fanned inflation, driving up the cost of living.
statements.test: True if official or peer-reviewed evidence attributes a measurable part of recent inflation to federal deficits. False if such evidence finds deficits had no inflationary effect. Cannot be determined if the evidence turns on contested economic models.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: Persistent large deficits have also pushed up interest rates, raising borrowing costs for home mortgages, auto loans, business loans, and almost any loan that you want to talk about.
statements.test: True if official or peer-reviewed evidence finds persistent deficits raised interest rates. False if such evidence finds no effect. Cannot be determined if the evidence turns on contested economic models.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: In 2026, interest rates on the national debt totaled $1.14 trillion, up 11 percent over last year.
statements.test: True if fiscal 2026 net interest on the national debt was about $1.14 trillion and about 11 percent above fiscal 2025. False if the official figures differ materially. Cannot be determined if no fiscal 2026 figure is published.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: Interest costs alone now exceed spending on the Department of national defense by $225 billion and even exceed Medicare expenses by $73 billion.
statements.test: True if fiscal 2026 net interest exceeded defense spending by about $225 billion and Medicare spending by about $73 billion. False if either gap differs materially or reverses. Cannot be determined if the fiscal 2026 figures are not published.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: That is why former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Admiral Michael Mullen famously declared that ``debt is the single biggest threat to [our] national security.''
statements.test: True if Adm. Michael Mullen, as Joint Chiefs chairman, said the national debt is the single biggest threat to national security. False if no such statement is on record and he said something different. Cannot be determined if no record of his words is found.

statements.speaker: Chuck Grassley
statements.context: Speaking on the Senate floor on November 16 about the Congressional Budget Office's annual review of fiscal 2026.
statements.quote: The Nation is on an unsustainable fiscal path.

statements.speaker: Dick Durbin
